Canonical Architecture Specification

Amira — Canonical Architecture Specification#

Session 4 output. This document is the canonical, present-tense description of how the Amira platform is built and operated. Every technology choice traces to a locked decision in /architecture/04-decisions.md (cited inline by ID); choices not deep-deliberated are clearly labeled "(default; revisit if constraints change)."

Scope: QDT's hosted Amira at amira.qdt.ai running in QDT's Azure subscription. The customer-environment redeployment model is described in §13 as a configuration of this same platform.

0. Visual overview#

A reader who only skims diagrams should still get the whole picture. The four diagrams below are the high-level views; §1–§14 are the prose contract underneath.

0.1 Azure resource inventory (procurement view)#

What gets provisioned in QDT's Azure subscription, plus the external services the platform depends on. This is the "what do I order" view — every box maps to a Terraform resource or a SaaS account.

Provisioning notes

  • Both AKS clusters use nested-virt-capable VM SKUs (Standard_D*s_v5 / Standard_E*s_v5 family) for any node pool hosting Kata-Firecracker pods (per RUNTIME-3, DEPLOY-2). The system node pools can use cheaper SKUs.
  • The Compliance-Mode Blob container lives in its own storage account so its locked retention policy is independent of the general-purpose Blob account (per AUDIT-1).
  • Postgres is single-region with point-in-time restore in v1; an HA replica is operational tuning (per RUNTIME-1 follow-up).
  • Authoritative DNS in the diagram shows Azure DNS as the working assumption (cleaner DNS-01 wildcard issuance than Namecheap's registrar-only DNS); the Namecheap-stays-authoritative alternative is operational, not architectural.

0.2 Layered logical architecture#

Top-down stack of logical layers — each box is a class of component, not a single pod. The dominant request flow is a top-down arrow; the data plane underneath everything is shared.

How to read this

  • Every user request enters at L1, threads down through L2 → L3, consults L4 (catalog / policy / identity), persists durable state through L5 into L6, and (for build / deploy / runtime) drives L7.
  • L8 is everything outside the platform's blast radius: model inference, package mirror, customer data, customer IdP.
  • Tenant isolation lives at L4 + L6 (RLS keyed on org_id, immutable session attributes set at connection open per PERSIST-5) and at L7 (namespace-per-org-per-app + NetworkPolicy default-deny per DEPLOY-2).

0.3 Network and ingress topology#

How a request actually travels — DNS, ingress, namespaces, egress.

Traffic terminations

  • amira.qdt.ai (UI, API, SSE) terminates at the platform cluster's nginx ingress.
  • <appslug>-<orgslug>.apps.amira.qdt.ai (preview + deployed apps, per BUILD-2) terminates at the workloads cluster's nginx ingress; one wildcard cert covers all (DNS-01).
  • Custom domains for deployed apps terminate at the same ingress with per-domain certs (HTTP-01).
  • .well-known/openapi.json for each deployed app is served by the same app pod (per API-GATEWAY-1).

Egress posture

  • Public-registry hostnames (npmjs.org, pypi.org) are blocked at the cluster egress; all installs route through Artifactory.
  • Each deployed app's NetworkPolicy allowlist is rendered from its spec's resolved skill set (per CROSS-4 layer 4) — only declared hostnames are reachable.

0.4 Per-component internals#

Four small diagrams for the heaviest components — the parts a reader needs to picture inside the box, not just outside it.

0.4.1 Agent runtime (single agent session)#

0.4.2 Audit pipeline (write path)#

0.4.3 Sandbox CRD (build / preview session)#

0.4.4 Deploy pipeline (Build → Production)#

1. System overview#

Amira is a multi-tenant SaaS platform that turns a natural-language specification into a running enterprise application, governed at every hand-off by an immutable audit trail. Users (organized into orgs and business-unit workspaces) interact with three pipeline agents — Spec, Build, and Deployment — to converge a spec, generate code, and ship a preview or a production deployment. Every deployed app can optionally be promoted to a companion agent that other users invoke via Ask Amira, inheriting the source app's permissions and audit boundary.

The platform runs on two AKS clusters in QDT's Azure subscription. amira-platform holds the control plane: the platform UI, the agent runtimes (Spec / Build / Deploy / Companion drivers), the durable workflow engine, the Postgres family that owns all tabular state + vector embeddings + audit ledger, the skill catalog, the identity layer, and the Grafana observability stack. amira-workloads runs two classes of pods on Kata-Firecracker microVMs: short-lived sandbox pods (build, preview, repo-import, skill dry-run) and long-lived deployed-customer-app pods, both governed by the upstream Kubernetes agent-sandbox CRD. The two clusters are connected via Azure VNet peering; the platform's DBOS workflow drives the workloads cluster's Argo Rollouts controller through its Kubernetes API. nginx ingress terminates amira.qdt.ai on the platform cluster and *.apps.amira.qdt.ai on the workloads cluster, with TLS via cert-manager + Let's Encrypt.

State sits in three substrates: PostgreSQL (Azure Database for PostgreSQL Flexible Server, with pgvector) is the system of record for all relational state, vector embeddings, durable workflow checkpoints, the per-service audit outboxes, and the hash-chained audit ledger; Azure Blob Storage (S3-compatible interface) holds spec exports, build artifacts, signatures, content-addressable build inputs, and the WORM-mode immutable Merkle anchors that seal the audit chain hourly; Azure Key Vault holds skill secrets and platform credentials, surfaced to pods through the external-secrets-operator sidecar pattern.

Identity propagates user-to-downstream via OAuth 2.0 OBO (RFC 8693 Token Exchange) with a cumulative act claim; every agent has its own service identity and obtains downstream tokens by exchanging the calling user's token, never by impersonating with a service-account credential. Skills are MCP servers with an Amira manifest overlay (role-gating, source-tier, secret refs, sideEffect-per-tool); the Build Agent resolves them at compile time into a build-plan.lock that is the audit-evidence handle for every build. Sandboxes are hardware-isolated by Kata-Firecracker; deployed apps run on the same microVM class with NetworkPolicy default-deny + spec-derived egress allowlists.

2. Component inventory#

2.1 User-facing surfaces#

Platform UI (amira.qdt.ai)#

  • Responsibility — Renders the Home portal, Specifications workspace, Canvas, Skills marketplace, Projects/Artifacts views, Settings, Ask Amira (full page + drawer), Project Governance, Approval surface, Audit Log. Ships as a Next.js (App Router) application that calls the Platform API for state.
  • Technology — Next.js + TypeScript + Tailwind. (default; matches the same stack the platform generates for customer apps, per BUILD-1.)
  • Data ownership — None. Pure consumer of Platform API + SSE streams.
  • Dependencies — Platform API, Platform IdP (OIDC redirect flow), Streaming endpoint (SSE).

Streaming endpoint (Server-Sent Events)#

  • Responsibility — One SSE connection per active Build/Spec session. Streams structured narration events (instruction-received, binding-resolved, file-written, compliance-re-evaluated, hot-reload-applied) from the agent runtime to the user's browser.
  • Technology — SSE over HTTP, terminated at nginx ingress on amira-platform (per STREAM-1).
  • Data ownership — None; it tails events from the agent runtime's in-process queue and from Postgres (LISTEN/NOTIFY on outbox tables for durable resumption).
  • Dependencies — Agent runtimes; Postgres LISTEN/NOTIFY for resume-after-disconnect.

2.2 Control-plane services (in amira-platform)#

Platform API#

  • Responsibility — REST + SSE surface for the UI; entry point for all user requests. Authenticates the request via session cookie, resolves (orgId, userId, role), sets immutable session attributes on Postgres connections, dispatches to the agent runtime, the skill catalog, or direct Postgres reads.
  • Technology — FastAPI (default; revisit if constraints change — the platform team is fluent in FastAPI; the Claude Agent SDK has first-class Python support; DBOS's natural shape is Python-decorated functions).
  • Data ownership — None directly; orchestrates calls into agent runtimes and Postgres.
  • Dependencies — Platform IdP, Postgres, Agent Runtimes, Skill Catalog, OPA, Grafana (OpenTelemetry export).

Agent runtimes (Spec / Build / Deploy / Companion drivers)#

  • Responsibility — Run the Claude Agent SDK's tool-use loop inside a DBOS-checkpointed workflow for each agent session. The Spec runtime drives spec elicitation, the Build runtime drives code edits via the file-ops API into the session's sandbox pod, the Deploy runtime drives the helm-render → image-build → Argo Rollouts → smoke-test pipeline, and Companion runtimes serve Ask-Amira invocations of deployed apps' synthesized MCP servers.
  • Technology — Claude Agent SDK (per RUNTIME-1, RUNTIME-2, RUNTIME-6) on top of DBOS workflows checkpointing into Postgres (per RUNTIME-1). Process model: long-lived Python worker pods pulling work from DBOS queues.
  • Data ownership — Owns each session's transient working state; durable state lives in DBOS workflow tables in Postgres.
  • Dependencies — Postgres (DBOS state), LLM provider via the adapter (default Anthropic API; env-toggle to Bedrock / Vertex / Foundry per LLM-6), Skill Catalog, MCP servers (skill backends), agent-sandbox CRD in workloads cluster, OPA, Azure Key Vault via external-secrets-operator, Audit Outbox tables.

DBOS workflow engine#

  • Responsibility — Durable execution of every Spec / Build / Deploy / Companion-register session and every continuous-compliance probe (per RUNTIME-1, ORCH-2, COMPLY-1). Step-checkpoints model calls, file-ops, MCP tool calls into Postgres so a worker crash resumes the session at the last checkpoint with replay-correctness.
  • Technology — DBOS Python (per RUNTIME-1) — Postgres-resident workflow engine; library, not a separate cluster.
  • Data ownership — DBOS-managed Postgres tables for workflow state (event history, queues, schedule).
  • Dependencies — Postgres only.

Skill Catalog + MCP Registry#

  • Responsibility — Stores every skill's MCP manifest + Amira overlay (role-gating, source-tier, secret refs, sideEffect- per-tool, signing key id, lifecycle state); resolves the per-build catalog into the build-plan.lock; gates community-tier promotions through the curation pipeline (per SKILL-1, SKILL-3, SKILL-5, SKILL-2). Also hosts companion-agent MCP-manifest entries (tier: deployment-proprietary).
  • Technology — In-process service inside Platform API (default; revisit if it needs to scale independently). Manifests live in Postgres; signed bundles and SBOMs in Azure Blob Storage.
  • Data ownership — skill, skill_version, skill_role_grant, skill_secret_binding, companion_agent_version, plus build_plan and build_plan_skill_binding rows.
  • Dependencies — Postgres, Azure Blob Storage, the curation-pipeline scanners (Socket + Snyk + custom prompt-injection scanner + Kata-Firecracker dry-run), Azure Key Vault for skill signing keys per tier (per SKILL-3).

Platform IdP (and identity layer)#

  • Responsibility — Authenticates platform users; federates from customer org IdPs (OIDC / SAML / OAuth 2.0); issues tokens that the agent runtime exchanges for downstream OBO tokens; is the OAuth 2.0 authorization server for the RFC 8693 token-exchange endpoint.
  • Technology — Hosted IdP that speaks OIDC / SAML / OAuth 2.0 with Token Exchange (RFC 8693). Concrete pick: open follow-up listed under the LLM-6 / IdP cluster (default working assumption: a managed IdP that supports federation + custom OIDC client registration + Token Exchange — Auth0 and WorkOS are the two realistic candidates given Token-Vault / OBO support; final pick is operations posture, not architecture).
  • Data ownership — User identity records; federation configurations per org; token-exchange grants. Mirrored into Postgres for the platform's user, org_membership, and org_idp_federation tables.
  • Dependencies — Postgres (cached identity), customer IdPs at federation time.

OPA policy engine#

  • Responsibility — Evaluates retrieval-plane authorization (chunks before LLM context, per PERSIST-5), deploy-gate threshold policies on CVE / dependency-policy / compliance-score outputs (per DEPLOY-4), and write-action gating against the spec capability graph (per AGENT-GUARD-1). Single OPA stack across both surfaces per PERSIST-5 follow-up.
  • Technology — Self-hosted OPA, Rego policies (per PERSIST-5 follow-up).
  • Data ownership — Policy bundles versioned per platform release; hot-reloaded.
  • Dependencies — Postgres for policy-input data lookups (workspace memberships, role grants); none external.

Audit Consumer#

  • Responsibility — Polls every service's outbox table with SELECT FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED (per ORCH-1), validates payloads against the per-kind validator registry, computes the next hash-chain row, and inserts into the audit ledger with the (orgId, projectSeq) carried through from the outbox row.
  • Technology — Single-process Python service. v1 ships one consumer (per ORCH-1); migration to per-partition consumers is flagged with a sustained-throughput trigger.
  • Data ownership — audit_ledger table; per-project audit sequence (audit_seq_<projectId> Postgres sequences).
  • Dependencies — Postgres only.

WORM Anchor Job#

  • Responsibility — Hourly job that reads the audit chain tip, computes the Merkle root, writes it to Azure Blob Immutable Compliance Mode in QDT's subscription, and records the anchor digest as the next ledger row's hash input (per AUDIT-1).
  • Technology — DBOS-scheduled workflow (default; revisit if constraints change).
  • Data ownership — Anchor blobs (Compliance-Mode locked, 7-year retention) and audit_anchor table rows.
  • Dependencies — Postgres, Azure Blob Storage.

Grafana / Loki / Tempo / Mimir stack#

  • Responsibility — Self-hosted observability for both clusters. Loki ingests platform + workloads logs; Tempo holds OpenTelemetry traces (including the redacted LLM-context trace store per OBS-3 + CROSS-6); Mimir holds metrics. Per-route SLIs computed from spans per OBS-2.
  • Technology — Grafana stack self-hosted in amira-platform (per OBS-3). Azure Monitor / Application Insights / Log Analytics rejected on cloud-portability grounds.
  • Data ownership — Trace and log retention policies (audit-bound views over LLM-context-redacted spans; retention separate from the 7-year audit-ledger window).
  • Dependencies — OpenTelemetry collector running as a DaemonSet in both clusters.

Reviewer Agent (linter)#

  • Responsibility — Runs the spec-side linter that scans free-text spec sections for vendor SDK imports, hostnames, and known function names (per CROSS-4 layer 2), surfacing structured warnings in the Spec UI (per CROSS-4 follow-up). Also evaluates the spec convergence rubric (per SPEC-1).
  • Technology — Library inside the Spec Agent runtime; not a separate service.
  • Data ownership — Linter pattern library (versioned with platform releases).
  • Dependencies — Spec Agent runtime, Spec capability graph (per SPEC-DECOMP-1).

2.3 Storage#

PostgreSQL (Azure Database for PostgreSQL Flexible Server, pgvector)#

  • Responsibility — System of record for all relational state + vector embeddings + DBOS workflow state + per-service audit outboxes + the audit ledger itself (per PERSIST-1, PERSIST-1 follow-ups, AUDIT-1).
  • Technology — Azure Database for PostgreSQL Flexible Server (per PERSIST-1 follow-ups). Self-hosted in-cluster Postgres operator rejected.
  • Data ownership — All platform tabular state (see §4).
  • Dependencies — None upstream; consumed by every control-plane service. Connection-pooling via PgBouncer / Supavisor sidecars open per RUNTIME-1 follow-up.

Azure Blob Storage#

  • Responsibility — S3-compatible object storage for spec exports, build artifacts, signatures, content-addressable build inputs (CAS keyed by (spec_hash, skill_versions, build_inputs) per BUILD-4), build-plan.lock blobs (per SKILL-2), and the WORM-mode immutable Merkle anchors (per AUDIT-1).
  • Technology — Azure Blob Storage in QDT's subscription, accessed through an S3-compatible interface (per BUILD-4 follow-ups, PERSIST-1 follow-ups). MinIO self-hosted rejected. The Compliance Mode container is a separate locked-policy container in the same subscription.
  • Data ownership — Spec / build / artifact / audit-anchor blobs.
  • Dependencies — Postgres holds pointers (content hashes) into Blob.

Azure Key Vault#

  • Responsibility — Holds skill secrets (three modes per SKILL-4: shared-platform, per-deployment, per-user-OAuth), platform service credentials, signing keys per skill tier (per SKILL-3), TLS material managed by cert-manager. Entra-ID-integrated for OBO-flow secret access (per SKILL-4 follow-up).
  • Technology — Azure Key Vault (per SKILL-4 follow-up). HashiCorp Vault rejected.
  • Data ownership — All non-data secret material.
  • Dependencies — Surfaced into pods via external-secrets-operator (default; revisit if constraints change). Pods never read Key Vault directly.

Azure Container Registry (ACR)#

  • Responsibility — Stores images Buildkit pushes for deployed customer apps and platform images.
  • Technology — ACR in QDT's subscription (per 00-context.md and DEPLOY-3).
  • Data ownership — Image manifests + layers.
  • Dependencies — Buildkit (push); Argo Rollouts / Helm (pull).

JFrog Artifactory (npm + PyPI + container mirror)#

  • Responsibility — Sole install source for every npm install and pip install issued by build sandboxes, preview pods, and deployed-app pods. Sigstore-compatible. Three-layer policy: mirror, plus behavioural / CVE / provenance scan, plus a per-deployment allowlist (per BUILD-6, BUILD-6 follow-ups).
  • Technology — JFrog Artifactory (per BUILD-6 follow-ups). Public registries refused at the cluster egress boundary.
  • Data ownership — Mirrored package versions + provenance metadata (Sigstore attestations).
  • Dependencies — Socket (behavioural scan), Trivy (CVE scan), and Sigstore cosign (provenance verification) called on every install (per BUILD-6 follow-ups).

2.4 Workload-cluster components (in amira-workloads)#

agent-sandbox CRD + SandboxWarmPool#

  • Responsibility — Provisions short-lived, hardware-isolated sandbox pods for Build sessions, Preview sessions, Repo-import pipelines, and Skill curation dry-runs. Warm pools keep cold-start under one second (per RUNTIME-3, BUILD-2).
  • Technology — Upstream Kubernetes agent-sandbox CRD (SIG-Apps ratified, March 2026). Kata-Firecracker RuntimeClass for every sandbox pod. AKS Pod Sandboxing enabled at cluster provisioning.
  • Data ownership — Pod-local ephemeral storage only; no durable state.
  • Dependencies — Kubernetes API, Artifactory mirror, Azure Key Vault (via external-secrets-operator), Platform API (file-ops API endpoint), GitHub (per-app repo two-way sync), HMR-aware framework containers (Next.js + FastAPI default per BUILD-1, BUILD-3).

Argo Rollouts controller#

  • Responsibility — Reconciles every Rollout CR for deployed customer apps. BlueGreen with prePromotionAnalysis runs the AC-runner + k6 NFR probes; abort-on-failure attributes back to the failing AC in audit (per DEPLOY-3, DEPLOY-5, DEPLOY-6).
  • Technology — Argo Rollouts (per DEPLOY-3, 00-context.md). Argo CD intentionally not adopted in v1 (per DEPLOY-3 — DBOS workflow and audit ledger are the single source of truth for deployment state).
  • Data ownership — Rollout CR state; AnalysisRun history (Kubernetes API state).
  • Dependencies — amira-workloads Kubernetes API, ACR (image pull), platform DBOS (drives the chart push and reads run state).

Buildkit pod#

  • Responsibility — Builds container images for deployed apps. Pulls dependencies through Artifactory; pushes images to ACR.
  • Technology — Open-source Buildkit on AKS (per DEPLOY-3). ACR Tasks rejected on cloud-portability grounds; off-cluster Buildkit- as-a-Service rejected (no need for an external dep on the deploy hot path).
  • Data ownership — Layer cache (ephemeral / configurable on a Persistent Volume).
  • Dependencies — Artifactory, ACR.

Companion-agent MCP servers#

  • Responsibility — Each deployed app that opted in to companion- agent provisioning at deploy time runs an MCP server alongside its app pod. The server exposes the deploy-time-resolved Build Plan tools, branded by the app's spec FRs (tool descriptions) and ACs (smoke tests). Calls land here from the platform Companion runtime on behalf of an Ask-Amira user; downstream queries run under the caller's OBO token (per AGENT-1, AGENT-2).
  • Technology — Synthesized SKILL.md + MCP server, generated at deploy step from the Build Plan (per AGENT-1 follow-ups). One companion-agent version per build (locked one-to-one).
  • Data ownership — None; downstream calls hit customer data sources or skill-backed MCP servers.
  • Dependencies — Skill Catalog (manifest entry), Azure Key Vault (skill secrets), Platform IdP (OBO exchange), customer data sources, Audit Outbox tables.

Deployed customer apps#

  • Responsibility — Run customer applications (Next.js + FastAPI by default) provisioned per org-<orgId>-app-<appId>-<env> namespace.
  • Technology — Per-stack Helm chart (initial: amira-app-nextjs-fastapi); Kata-Firecracker pods; per-namespace NetworkPolicy default-deny + spec-derived egress allowlist (per CROSS-4 layer 4).
  • Data ownership — Customer-app-owned tables in per-app database (provisioning model is open; per PERSIST-1 follow-up).
  • Dependencies — Skills (MCP servers, customer warehouses), Artifactory, ACR, Azure Key Vault.

4. Persistence layer#

The platform operates one Postgres family, one S3-compatible object store, and one secret store. Three operational substrates total — by design, to keep the operations surface minimal (per RUNTIME-1, PERSIST-1).

4.1 PostgreSQL (Azure Database for PostgreSQL Flexible Server)#

Holds tabular state, vector embeddings, durable workflow state, audit outboxes, and the audit ledger itself. Single instance for v1; logical separation by table; PgBouncer / Supavisor sized for the workflow + application + audit triple-workload (specifics open per RUNTIME-1 follow-up).

Table family What it holds Retention Consistency
org, org_membership, user, org_idp_federation, role, role_grant Identity + tenancy graph Lifetime of org + 90 days post-deletion (default) Strong; RLS keyed by org_id
workspace (BU), workspace_membership Sub-tenant grouping inside an org Same as org Strong; RLS keyed by org_id (BU enforced via workspace_id predicate)
project, project_governance, project_collaborator Project records, governance role assignments, exposure scope Lifetime of project + archival window Strong; RLS
spec_version, spec_capability_graph, decision_point, gap, kb_attachment, spec_skill_reference Living spec doc, structured capability graph (per SPEC-DECOMP-1), knowledge base Lifetime of project; immutable per version Strong
approval_request, approval_signature Approval routing + e-signature records 7 years (audit-bound) Append-only
build, build_plan, build_plan_skill_binding, build_artifact_pointer Per-build state; pointers into Blob CAS Lifetime of project Append-only per build
compliance_matrix_row, compliance_evidence, compliance_score_history Per-FR compliance evidence + scores Lifetime of project Mutable (continuous re-eval per COMPLY-1) with history
deploy_run, deploy_smoke_result, deploy_companion_pin Deploy lifecycle + AC-tagged smoke results + paired companion-agent version pin (per DEPLOY-5) Lifetime of project Append-only
skill, skill_version, skill_role_grant, skill_secret_binding, skill_signature, skill_lifecycle Skill catalog + tier-signed manifests Lifetime of skill (immutable per version per SKILL-5) Append-only per version
companion_agent_version, companion_agent_active_pointer Companion-agent registry; active-pointer per source app Lifetime of source app Append-only versions; pointer flip is the rollback primitive
kb_doc, kb_chunk (with pgvector), kb_promotion Knowledge-base attachments; embeddings; per-KB-promotion scope (private / team / org per KB-PROMOTION-1) Lifetime of project Mutable
DBOS workflow tables (managed) Workflow event histories, queues, schedules Per workflow lifetime + tunable retention Strong (DBOS guarantees)
Per-service _outbox tables Audit events pending consumption (per ORCH-1) Until consumed (TTL on consumed rows) Append-only
audit_ledger (monthly partitions) Hash-chained ledger; one row per audit event with (orgId, projectSeq) index 7 years (regulatory) Append-only with hash-chain integrity
audit_anchor Hourly Merkle anchor records (digest, blob URI) 7 years Append-only
llm_call, llm_call_metering OpenTelemetry-derived per-call metering rows (per LLM-4); aggregated views over 13 months (default; revisit if billing posture changes) Append-only
audit_kind_validator Per-kind presence-rule registry (per AUDIT-2) Lifetime of platform Strong

Tenancy isolation — Postgres RLS enforces row visibility keyed by org_id. Snowflake-style immutable session attributes (per PERSIST-5) are set on every connection at session open; generated SQL or tool calls inside the session cannot rewrite them. Workspace (BU) isolation is a second predicate (workspace_id) inside the same RLS mechanism.

Backup story — Azure Database for PostgreSQL Flexible Server manages backups; geo-redundant backup with 35-day point-in-time restore is the default working assumption (default; revisit if constraints change). The audit-ledger immutability story does not depend on Postgres backup — it is owned by the WORM anchor in Azure Blob Compliance Mode (§4.3, §10).

4.2 Vector embeddings (pgvector inside the same Postgres)#

Per PERSIST-1, pgvector is the only vector backend. Embeddings live on the same Postgres instance — kb_chunk.embedding, spec_capability_graph.embedding (where useful for retrieval), companion-agent context indexes. Pinecone / Weaviate / LanceDB / Chroma are out of scope.

4.3 Object storage (Azure Blob, S3-compatible interface)#

Container What it holds Retention Consistency
specs Spec exports (PRD / SOW / cost / risk PDFs per 2.5) Lifetime of spec version Read-after-write
artifacts Built deployable bundles, source bundles, deploy reports Lifetime of project + archival window Read-after-write
cas Content-addressable build inputs keyed by (spec_hash, skill_versions, build_inputs) (per BUILD-4) Lifetime of project (cache-evictable on TTL where the row is no longer referenced from a live build row) Read-after-write
lockfiles build-plan.lock blobs (per SKILL-2) Lifetime of project Read-after-write
signatures E-signature blob payloads (full signed envelope, audit-cross-referenced) 7 years Read-after-write
audit-anchors (Compliance Mode) Hourly Merkle anchors (per AUDIT-1, PERSIST-2 + AUDIT-1) 7 years, locked policy WORM (immutable; cannot be modified by Microsoft, by QDT operators, or anyone)
skill-bundles Signed MCP-server bundles + SBOM attestations per skill version Lifetime of skill version (immutable per SKILL-5) Read-after-write

Code never binds to provider-specific SDKs; everything goes through the S3-compatible interface (per PERSIST-1) so re-pointing to MinIO or another provider is a configuration change.

4.4 Generated codebase storage#

Two layers, both required (per BUILD-4, BUILD-4 follow-ups):

  • User-facing layer: per-project Git repository at GitHub under a single QDT-managed Git org (per BUILD-4 follow-ups). One repo per app. Branch = spec version; tag = build number. The Build Agent's file-ops API writes to the sandbox pod and commits + pushes through a two-way sync.
  • Internal layer: content-addressable storage in Blob (cas container) keyed by the build-input triple. Reproducibility is a contract, not best-effort: rebuilding (spec_hash, skill_versions, build_inputs) retrieves the same artifact bytes.

Time-travel UI in Canvas is Phase 2 (per BUILD-4 follow-ups).

4.5 Secrets#

Azure Key Vault holds all secret material — skill secrets in three modes (shared-platform, per-deployment, per-user-OAuth per SKILL-4), platform service credentials, and tier-signing keys (QDT release key, deployment-admin keys, community-publisher keys per SKILL-3). Pods read secrets via the external-secrets-operator sidecar pattern (per 00-context.md "Secrets" + SKILL-4); no pod embeds secret values in image, code, or environment files at build time. Secrets never reach LLM context (per LLM-5).

5. Identity, auth, and authorization#

5.1 Sign-in and session#

Platform users authenticate against the Platform IdP at amira.qdt.ai. The IdP federates from each org's customer IdP (OIDC / SAML / OAuth 2.0) at org-onboarding time; users sign in through their company SSO and land in their org's workspace (per IDA-2, MTEN-1). Just-in-time user provisioning creates the user + org_membership rows on first login.

Sessions are issued as secure, HttpOnly cookies bound to the IdP-issued ID token + refresh token. Step-up MFA is required for sensitive actions: deploy, e-signature, secret-binding configuration (per IDA-5). PATs are a strict subset of user capabilities — they cannot sign approvals, read skill secrets, or trigger writes against external systems (per IDA-5).

5.2 Authorization at request time#

Every request reaches the Platform API with a session-resolved identity (orgId, userId, roles). The Platform API:

  1. Sets immutable session attributes on the Postgres connection (SET LOCAL app.org_id = …, app.user_id = …, plus a no-rewrite guard per PERSIST-5).
  2. Enforces tenancy via Postgres RLS keyed on org_id, with a second workspace_id predicate for BU scope (per IDA-2).
  3. Calls OPA at the retrieval plane for policy decisions on data chunks before they reach LLM context (per PERSIST-5 follow-up).

access = (tenant_match) ∧ (role_grant) — these are independent dimensions (per IDA-2). Single composite enums are rejected.

5.3 Identity propagation to downstream systems (OBO)#

Every platform agent (Spec, Build, Deploy, Companion) holds its own service identity registered with the Platform IdP. Downstream calls against user-permissioned data — customer warehouses, skill MCP servers, the platform's own Postgres for user-context queries — go through OAuth 2.0 OBO via RFC 8693 Token Exchange. The user's session token is exchanged for a downstream token whose sub is the user and whose act claim is the agent (cumulative for multi-hop delegation, capped at six elements per AUDIT-2). Service- account-with-tenant-cookie is permanently rejected (per IDA-3).

For long-running agent jobs that outlive the originating session, the platform uses the IdP's refresh-token flow (per IDA-3 follow-up). On refresh failure the workflow checkpoints and pauses; the user gets a re-auth notification; on re-auth the workflow resumes from the last checkpoint with a fresh OBO token. Capability-token- fallback and background-service-identity are rejected.

5.4 Skill resolution via OBO#

When the agent invokes a skill MCP server, the runtime obtains an OBO token for the call. Inside the skill server:

  • shared-platform secrets are resolved from Key Vault by the vault sidecar — one secret value for all callers (per SKILL-4).
  • per-deployment secrets are resolved per org, keyed by the caller's org_id (deployment admins set the value at install time).
  • per-user-OAuth secrets require the calling user to have completed the skill's OAuth flow; the user's stored skill-token is fetched via the vault sidecar. First-call UX: if the user hasn't authorized, the agent surfaces a "connect " step inline.

Audit attribution is the three-field actor model: userId, agentId, serviceId, with causedBy UUID pointing to the upstream audit row (per IDA-3, AUDIT-2). Companion-agent calls record the source app's agentId and the calling user's userId, with the act chain reflecting the end-to-end delegation (per AGENT-2).

5.5 Customer-environment IdP federation#

When Amira is redeployed into a customer environment (§13), the customer's IdP becomes the Platform IdP for that deployment. The customer's directory drives users + roles directly; federation is not needed because there is only one IdP. The agent service identities and OBO flow are reconfigured against the customer IdP. Any IdP that speaks OIDC / SAML / OAuth 2.0 + Token Exchange is supported — Mars's Entra ID is the reference case, with Microsoft Entra Agent ID as the standardized OBO-for-agents pattern (per 00-context.md "Identity and authorization").

6. Agent runtime#

6.1 SDK and execution model#

Every agent (Spec, Build, Deploy, Companion driver) runs the Claude Agent SDK as the inner tool-use loop, embedded inside a DBOS workflow that checkpoints into the platform Postgres (per RUNTIME-1, AGENT-TOPO-1). Workflows are decorated Python functions; model calls, tool calls, and MCP-server calls are step-checkpointed so a worker crash resumes at the last successful step with replay- correctness. Stateless request/response is rejected for sessions that routinely span many minutes and many tool calls.

Day-one topology is single-agent ReAct loop with tools (per AGENT-TOPO-1). A verifier sub-agent (compliance re-eval running async alongside the main loop) is added when the Compliance Matrix re-eval starves the main loop's context budget — measurable trigger, data-driven introduction, not day-one. Replit-style manager/editor/verifier triads are deferred until single-agent error rate is unacceptable.

6.2 Per-instruction routing#

A small classifier model runs upfront on every chat instruction, parallelized with context assembly so latency is hidden. Output is a discrete intent label (edit / binding-or-schema / out-of-scope) that dispatches to the specialized sub-agent path (per RUNTIME-4). Misclassifications surface as out-of-scope blocks or wrong-tool retries; both are observable and audit-emitting.

6.3 Code-edit modality (Build Agent)#

Model emits search-replace blocks (or unified diff with elision); a deterministic apply function does str.replace(search, replace) against the file's current contents in-process and fails fast on no-match or ambiguous-match (per RUNTIME-2). On failure the model gets a structured error and re-emits with the current file contents in context. Apply-failure rate is an SLI; retries emit structured audit events. The file-ops API is the single seam the apply backend lives behind — future swap-out (e.g., to self-hosted Morph) is a single-point change. Aider's published 26% → 59% improvement from emit/apply separation is the on-record reason this shape is locked.

6.4 Context and compaction#

Long Build Agent sessions use the Claude Agent SDK's default 5-stage compaction pipeline (budget reduction → snip → microcompact → context collapse → auto-compact) for v1 (per RUNTIME-6). Custom per-stage budgets are introduced only if dogfood telemetry shows the SDK defaults wedge for QDT's edit patterns. Naive truncation and summary-then-resume are rejected.

6.5 Streaming and resumability#

Server-Sent Events from amira-platform to the user's browser, one connection per session (per STREAM-1). Narration events follow a structured event schema: instruction-received, binding-resolved, file-written, compliance-re-evaluated, hot-reload-applied. User pause / resume / cancel use separate REST endpoints. WebSocket multiplexer and event-sourced read model are rejected as v1 over-scope. The DBOS workflow + Postgres LISTEN/NOTIFY on outbox tables enables disconnected-then-reconnected clients to resume streaming.

6.6 Tool calling#

Every tool the agent invokes is an MCP tool (per SKILL-1). The agent runtime resolves tools at compile time through the Build Plan lockfile (Build / Deploy paths) or at session start through the calling org's catalog view (Spec / Companion paths). At runtime the runtime layer:

  1. Re-validates the calling identity's role intersects the bound role; mismatch fails closed (per SKILL-2).
  2. Looks up the per-tool sideEffect annotation. read tools execute without confirmation; write and external-write tools prompt the inline-confirm UX (per AGENT-3, AGENT-3 follow-up).
  3. Acquires an OBO token for the call (per AGENT-2 follow-up — always-runtime token-exchange per call; sealed capability tokens rejected).
  4. Calls the MCP server.
  5. Writes a per-call audit event to the runtime's outbox (kind tied to the tool's side effect).

6.7 MCP integration#

MCP is the wire format for all skills (per SKILL-1). The Skill Catalog stores manifests (MCP standard fields + Amira overlay: role-gating, source-tier, secret-refs, app-agent-provenance, lifecycle-state, sideEffect-per-tool, signing-key-id, manifest-schema-version). Non-MCP sources (proprietary internal APIs, Anthropic Skills, raw OpenAPI) wrap behind QDT-maintained MCP adapters. Non-immutable-publish MCP servers are wrapped: QDT pins a content-hash version per fetch and re-publishes under a stable Amira-managed version (per SKILL-1 follow-ups).

The Build Agent code-gen stage reads the resolved MCP endpoint from the lockfile, never from a runtime registry lookup. Drift between build-time and runtime endpoints is detectable as a content-hash mismatch on the lockfile.

6.8 Cost-and-concurrency posture#

Per-org concurrency limits (one Build Agent session per user at a time within an org; org-level concurrent-user limit configurable per subscription tier) + dynamic model-tier selection inside the agent runtime: Haiku-class for classification / compliance scans / out-of-scope checks, top-class for code-edit + spec elicitation (per COST-CONC-1). Per-org BYOK (per LLM-6) is the release valve when an org wants to lift platform-imposed limits using its own credentials.

LLM caching is hierarchical via Anthropic's cache_control blocks (per LLM-CACHE-1): system prompt + tool catalog cached per session (long TTL); spec doc cached per spec version (invalidated on lock); file-tree snapshot cached per build (invalidated on lockfile change); tool-call results cached per (skill-id, version, args) tuple. The env-var-toggle adapter preserves identical cache_control semantics when migrating to Bedrock / Vertex / Foundry.

6.9 Guardrails#

Layered defense-in-depth (per AGENT-GUARD-1):

  1. Per-tool sideEffect annotation (deterministic primary classifier; manifest-validator rejects unannotated tools at the catalog gate per AGENT-3 follow-up).
  2. OPA gates write actions against the spec's capability graph (per SPEC-DECOMP-1).
  3. Runtime egress NetworkPolicy allowlist blocks calls to undeclared hostnames (per CROSS-4 layer 4).
  4. Inline LLM-judge confirmation for external-write actions.
  5. Kata-Firecracker per-pod isolation bounds blast radius.

6.10 Out-of-scope detection#

Layered (per ORCH-4): capability-membership check against the spec's capability graph (deterministic) → LLM judge with a structured rubric for ambiguous cases the graph can't resolve. All decisions emit audit events distinguishing first-pass blocks from second-pass blocks. The spec capability graph is populated by the Spec Agent at finalization (per ORCH-4 follow-up).

7. Build & preview infrastructure#

7.1 Sandbox primitive#

Every Build, Spec, Preview, and Repo-import session runs as one pod managed by the upstream Kubernetes agent-sandbox CRD on the amira-workloads cluster, with SandboxWarmPool for sub-second cold-starts (per RUNTIME-3, BUILD-2). The RuntimeClass is Kata-Firecracker: hardware-isolated microVMs with KVM-backed per-pod kernel + network namespace isolation. AKS Pod Sandboxing is enabled at cluster provisioning; node pools come from nested-virt- capable VM SKUs (Standard_D*s_v5 / Standard_E*s_v5 family). External Sandboxes-as-a-Service (Vercel Sandbox, E2B, Modal, StackBlitz WebContainers) and container-only kernel-shared isolation are both rejected (per RUNTIME-3).

7.2 Warm pools and stack templates#

Each warm pool prebuilds a sandbox image per supported stack. v1 ships one pool: Next.js (App Router) + FastAPI (per BUILD-1). Adding a stack costs one Helm chart + warm-pool template + file-ops adapter + dependency-policy bundle + AC-runner adapter (estimated ~1 dev-month at v1 maturity per BUILD-1). Pool sizing is operational tuning (per RUNTIME-3 follow-ups, BUILD-2 follow-ups).

7.3 File-ops API and HMR#

The Build Agent never touches the sandbox filesystem directly; all mutations go through the file-ops API endpoint exposed by each sandbox pod. The API performs atomic write-then-fsync-then-rename operations (per BUILD-3); the framework's file watcher picks up the rename and triggers HMR — Turbopack for Next.js, uvicorn-hmr for FastAPI. When a change can't be HMR'd in place (large refactor, dependency install, schema change), the dev server restarts and the UI surfaces a rebuilding (full restart) state distinct from in-place HMR.

The platform does not own the bundler. The framework's dev server rebuilds and notifies; the file-ops API is the agent's only contract.

7.4 Preview hostnames#

Hostname pattern: <appslug>-<orgslug>.apps.amira.qdt.ai (per BUILD-2). One wildcard cert covers the namespace; nginx ingress in amira-workloads terminates the connection and routes to the sandbox pod's preview Service.

Warm-pool readiness is surfaced to the UI as a "preview ready" state when the slot is allocated and the dev server reports ready; the user does not see an opaque spinner (per BUILD-2).

7.5 Terminal / console#

The Console / build log UI subscribes to a structured-event stream emitted by the Build Agent (instruction received, binding resolved, file written, compliance re-evaluated, hot-reload latency, apply errors). Events are streamed over SSE (per STREAM-1) and persisted to Loki for retrospective view; audit-relevant events also flow to the audit ledger via the agent's outbox.

7.6 Lifecycle and cleanup#

Sandbox pods are claimed from the warm pool on session start, returned to the pool on session end (or torn down if customized beyond reset), and time out after a configurable inactivity window (default; revisit if constraints change). The CRD owns the lifecycle. Build-session checkpoints + Git two-way sync (per features 14.5, 14.8) preserve user work across pod recycles.

7.7 Repo-import pipeline (reverse engineering)#

Repo imports run inside the same agent-sandbox CRD pod class (Kata-Firecracker per RUNTIME-3, REVENG-1). The pipeline does AST-walk + framework-detection heuristics + LLM inference of FRs/NFRs/ACs with provenance back to source files. Sandboxed- execution probes (running the imported app) are rejected — slow plus side-effect risk. CodeQL / Semgrep are over-scope for v1. Imported non-Next/FastAPI stacks are host-only per BUILD-1 — the platform can run them and serve them under the same hostname pattern, but the Build Agent's full editing capability (HMR-driven iteration, AC-driven smoke tests, compliance probes) is degraded until that stack is added to v1's supported set.

8. Deployment infrastructure#

8.1 Deploy orchestration engine#

DBOS for the platform-side workflow + Helm + Argo Rollouts for the K8s deploy step itself (per DEPLOY-3). Argo CD is intentionally not adopted in v1 — the DBOS workflow + audit ledger is the single source of truth for what got deployed; adding GitOps reconciliation would create a second source of truth.

8.2 Per-stack Helm charts#

QDT owns one Helm chart per supported stack. v1 ships amira-app-nextjs-fastapi (per BUILD-1). Each chart templates the customer app's Rollout CR, Service, Ingress, NetworkPolicy (default-deny + spec-derived egress allowlist per CROSS-4), and ResourceQuota. Charts are versioned and live alongside the platform code; chart upgrades flow through the platform release process.

Per-app deploys are Helm releases in org-<orgId>-app-<appId>-<env> namespaces. Helm release history backs the v1.0 forward-only rollback posture (helm rollback <release> <revision>).

8.3 Image build#

Buildkit pod inside amira-workloads. Pulls dependencies through JFrog Artifactory (the only sanctioned source per BUILD-6). Pushes to ACR. Each install is scanned: Socket (behavioural malware) + Trivy (CVE) + Sigstore cosign (provenance verification) per BUILD-6 follow-ups. ACR Tasks rejected (cloud-portability); off-cluster Buildkit-as-a-Service rejected (no need for an external dep on the deploy hot path).

8.4 Argo Rollouts BlueGreen with AC-tagged smoke tests#

Argo Rollouts BlueGreen brings up the new ReplicaSet, runs prePromotionAnalysis, and either flips the Service selector (success) or aborts and keeps the previous active (failure). The prePromotionAnalysis AnalysisTemplate runs:

  • The AC-runner — a custom Python runner (per DEPLOY-3) that consumes the spec's AC DSL (per SPEC-DECOMP-1) and executes each AC as a smoke test against the new ReplicaSet. The mockup's period-end recon ±$0.5M is literally AC-1 from the FinIQ spec (per DEPLOY-6).
  • k6 for spec-NFR latency probes (per DEPLOY-6, OBS-2).
  • OPA Rego deploy-gate policies (per DEPLOY-4) consuming scanner outputs (Trivy CVE scan, dependency-policy bundle results from BUILD-6) and the latest compliance-score from the Compliance Matrix. Failures block traffic flip and emit AC-tagged audit events with the failing rule.

When an AC changes, the smoke test is regenerated from the new AC by default and an audit event ac-changed-test-regenerated is emitted (per DEPLOY-6 follow-up). Manual override is available via PR with audit trail.

8.5 Domain provisioning#

  • Default app domains: wildcard *.apps.amira.qdt.ai. One wildcard cert in amira-workloads's nginx ingress, issued by cert-manager + Let's Encrypt via DNS-01 (per 00-context.md). external-dns watches Ingress objects and creates the corresponding DNS records.
  • Custom domains for deployed apps: opt-in per app. Per-domain Ingress, per-domain cert via HTTP-01.
  • Hostname pattern (per BUILD-2): <appslug>-<orgslug>.apps.amira.qdt.ai — sub-domain per app scoped to org.

8.6 TLS#

cert-manager with ClusterIssuer; Let's Encrypt as the default issuer (production), with a staging issuer available for non-prod (per 00-context.md). Wildcard cert via DNS-01; per-app custom domain certs via HTTP-01.

8.7 Companion agent registration#

After the Service-selector flip succeeds, the deploy DBOS workflow synthesizes the SKILL.md + MCP server from the resolved Build Plan tools, the spec's FRs (as natural-language tool descriptions), and the spec's ACs (as smoke tests), and publishes a companion_agent_version row in the Skill Catalog at tier deployment-proprietary (per AGENT-1, SKILL-3, AGENT-1 follow-ups). The companion-agent version is locked one-to-one with the build version. The companion_agent_active_pointer for the source app flips atomically with the deployed-app traffic switch.

Companion-agent provisioning is opt-in at deploy (per AGENT-1). The deploy modal carries a "register companion agent" toggle with a sensible default per project type. Synthesis happens at the deploy step (manifest reflects deploy-environment bindings, not build-time bindings, per AGENT-1 follow-ups). Authoring affordance is pure auto for v1; explicit prompt customization is Phase 2.

8.8 Rollback model#

v1.0 ships forward-only via helm rollback <release> <revision> — the rollback UI surface in Canvas / Projects is "redeploy previous build," not "atomic rollback" (per DEPLOY-5). v1.5 adds Argo Rollouts BlueGreen rollback with the paired companion-agent version-pin flip atomicity: the Skill Catalog stores both old and new agent versions, and rollback flips the active pointer atomically with the app's Service selector flip. Canary-with-progressive-traffic is rejected for v1.x (BlueGreen suits AC-driven smoke tests better).

8.9 External API exposure (per app)#

Thin sidecar (v1) per API-GATEWAY-1. Per-app API tokens issued through Project Governance; spec-derived OpenAPI manifest at https://<appslug>-<orgslug>.apps.amira.qdt.ai/.well-known/openapi.json; every external call lands in the audit ledger tagged external-api; audience-RBAC reuses the spec's role surface. No quotas UI, no developer portal, no mTLS, no monetization in v1. Full API management (Kong / Apigee parity) is Phase 2.

9. Event/orchestration architecture#

9.1 Eventing backbone#

Postgres outbox + idempotency-keyed consumer (per ORCH-1):

  • Each platform service (agent runtimes, Skill Catalog, Approval service, Deploy workflow, etc.) owns an <service>_outbox table next to its business tables. Business writes and outbox writes commit in the same Postgres transaction (atomicity).
  • One global Audit Consumer in v1 polls every outbox via SELECT FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED. Consumer outage delays audit visibility but never blocks business writes.
  • Per-project monotonic sequence numbers are allocated from a Postgres sequence per project (audit_seq_<projectId>) at outbox-row insert. Audit ledger rows carry (orgId, project_seq) as a unique index for fast intra-project forensic queries.
  • Cross-table commit-order is not preserved at the relay; cross-event ordering uses the causedBy causation DAG (per AUDIT-2), not WAL order.

WAL-tailing, multi-domain consumers, and UUID-only-no-sequence are rejected for v1 with explicit migration triggers documented (per ORCH-1: WAL-tail when sustained chain-write throughput exceeds ~1k events/sec for a rolling 24h window; per-project chain sharding when sustained throughput approaches the ~5k events/sec single- writer ceiling). Cross-region fanout (Kafka / NATS JetStream) is deferred until cross-region demand is real.

9.2 Three-agent pipeline orchestration (Spec → Build → Deploy → Companion)#

Per-phase DBOS workflows with handoff via durable signal (per ORCH-2). Each phase is its own DBOS workflow; the handoff envelope binds the phases together durably.

Single-megaworkflow-spans-project-lifecycle is rejected; per-phase fits DBOS's natural shape and gives each phase its own retry / error-handling story (per ORCH-2).

9.3 Hand-off envelopes (per RUNTIME-7)#

Hand-off envelopes are the only way one phase invokes the next. Each carries the locked inputs the next phase needs and is recorded as an audit event:

Hand-off Envelope contents Audit kind
Spec → Build frozen spec hash, signed approval ID, resolved build-plan.lock content hash build-handoff
Build → Deploy frozen spec hash, signed approval ID, build N, lockfile hash, image digest deploy-handoff
Deploy → Companion-register build N, env, deployment ID, opt-in flag companion-handoff

The Build Agent reads only from the Spec → Build envelope; references outside it are rejected. Bare-database-state-machine and approval-ID- only hand-offs are rejected because they don't bind the resolved build plan to the approval (per RUNTIME-7).

9.4 Continuous compliance probing#

Hybrid event-triggered + scheduled (per COMPLY-1). Probes run on event signals (skill version change, data-source schema change, deploy completion) for fast feedback, with a 6h scheduled timer as backstop. Probes are AC-tagged k6 jobs running against deployed apps. Failures recompute the compliance score and emit audit events.

9.5 KB promotion lifecycle#

User-initiated promotion with three scope levels: private → team → org-wide (per KB-PROMOTION-1). Org admins can demote or remove. Cross-org promotion rejected.

9.6 Fork lineage#

A forked project carries a forkedFromProjectId lineage edge for audit traversal. Spec content + governance role assignments are inherited; build / deploy / approvals / KB reset (per FORK-LINEAGE-1).

10. Observability and audit#

10.1 Logging, tracing, metrics#

Self-hosted Grafana stack in amira-platform (per OBS-3): Loki for logs, Tempo for traces, Mimir for metrics. OpenTelemetry collector runs as a DaemonSet in both clusters and forwards to the stack. Azure Monitor / Application Insights / Log Analytics are rejected on cloud-portability grounds.

LLM-call telemetry is OpenTelemetry middleware emitting spans tagged with (orgId, userId, projectId, agentRole, callType, model, cached-read, cache-write, uncached, latency, status) (per LLM-4). Spans land in Tempo; aggregations build per-org / per-project / per-agent / per-call-type cost + latency views (also surfaced in billing / Settings UI).

10.2 Trace store, redaction, and audit-bound view#

Tool-call results land in Tempo with content redaction tags applied to PII / RLS-marked rows before LLM context (per CROSS-6 follow-up, LLM-5). The LLM sees the redacted view; the trace store retains the full content but engineers see only the redacted view by default. Audit-bound roles can request the un-redacted view; the request itself is an audit event. The trace store's retention is separate from the 7-year audit-ledger window (default; revisit if constraints change).

10.3 Per-route SLIs and NFR compliance#

Live per-route SLIs computed from OpenTelemetry spans (P50 / P95 first-token, dashboard load, voice end-to-end, errors per 1k) per LLM-4 schema (per OBS-2). k6 scheduled probes every 6h (per COMPLY-1) for AC-tagged compliance NFR checks against deployed apps. Breaches trigger alerts and emit audit events.

10.4 Audit ledger and immutability#

Substrate — Hash-chained Postgres ledger + Azure Blob Immutable Compliance Mode as the WORM Merkle anchor (per AUDIT-1, PERSIST-2 + AUDIT-1).

  • Each ledger row stores prev_hash + row_hash. The chain is intrinsically serial — one writer, regardless of how many consumers feed it.
  • Hourly job reads the chain tip, computes the Merkle root, writes it to Azure Blob Immutable Compliance Mode in QDT's subscription. The anchor digest is recorded as the next ledger row's hash input.
  • 7-year retention is enforced by Azure Blob's locked policy; retention can be extended but not shortened.
  • The immutability cannot be overridden by Microsoft support, by QDT operators, or by anyone (per AUDIT-1).
  • An external regulator audit is satisfied by handing over the ledger export + the anchor blob set; chain integrity is verifiable end-to-end. SEC 17a-4(f) / FINRA 4511(c) / CFTC 1.31(c) defensible.

EventStoreDB and distributed-ledger products are rejected as operational overhead with no compliance benefit. MinIO self-hosted is rejected. Public anchor publication is not a v1 feature; revisit only if a regulator or customer specifically asks (per PERSIST-2 + AUDIT-1).

10.5 Audit attribution#

Three-field actor (userId, agentId, serviceId, any nullable per kind with per-kind validator) + causedBy UUID pointer + (orgId, projectSeq) for intra-project ordering (per AUDIT-2). Causation DAG stored as parent-pointer chain in Postgres (UUID column, indexed); traversal via recursive CTE. No separate graph database. Wire format between services is RFC 8693 act-chain, capped at 6 elements.

Audit kinds are an extensible schema. Mockup seeds twelve representative kinds; production schema is open-ended with a per-kind validator registry (per 00-context.md "Audit and lineage"). Treating "twelve" as a closed set is a mockup-as-truth trap.

10.6 Correlation: a single user action threading through every component#

When a user fires "lock spec for e-signature" in Canvas:

  1. Platform API receives the request with session identity → emits audit userId=user, agentId=null, serviceId=platform-api, kind=spec-lock-requested, causedBy=null.
  2. Spec Agent runtime exchanges the user's token via OBO → emits audit userId=user, agentId=spec, serviceId=spec-runtime, kind=spec-locked, causedBy=spec-lock-requested.
  3. Approval routing notifies the authorized approver → emits audit agentId=null, serviceId=approval-router, kind=approval-routed, causedBy=spec-locked.
  4. Approver e-signs → audit userId=approver, serviceId=approval-ui, kind=approval-signed, causedBy=approval-routed.
  5. Build Agent receives hand-off envelope → audit agentId=build, kind=build-handoff, causedBy=approval-signed.
  6. … and so on through build-plan-resolved, file-edit, deploy-handoff, etc.

Recursive-CTE traversal of the causedBy DAG retrieves the entire thread. Per-project monotonic projectSeq orders events deterministically within a project. The act-chain on the wire format carries the delegation chain through external systems.

11. Kubernetes topology#

11.1 Two-cluster split#

Two AKS clusters in QDT's Azure subscription (per DEPLOY-2 / DEPLOY-1):

amira-platform cluster#

  • Runs: Platform API + UI server, Agent runtime worker pods, DBOS scheduler / queue runner, Skill Catalog service, Platform IdP client, OPA, Audit Consumer, WORM Anchor scheduled job, Grafana / Loki / Tempo / Mimir, OpenTelemetry collector DaemonSet, external-secrets-operator, cert-manager, external-dns, nginx ingress.
  • Termination: amira.qdt.ai (platform UI, API, SSE).

amira-workloads cluster#

  • Runs: agent-sandbox CRD controller + warm pools, Argo Rollouts controller, Buildkit pod, deployed customer-app pods, companion-agent MCP-server pods, OpenTelemetry collector DaemonSet, external-secrets-operator, cert-manager, external-dns, nginx ingress.
  • Termination: *.apps.amira.qdt.ai (deployed apps + previews).

The two clusters are connected via Azure VNet peering. The platform cluster's DBOS workflow drives the workloads cluster's Argo Rollouts + agent-sandbox resources through the workloads cluster's Kubernetes API over the peered network.

11.2 Namespaces#

In amira-platform#

  • platform-system — control-plane services, OPA, IdP integration.
  • platform-data — Audit Consumer, WORM Anchor job, DBOS workers, external-secrets-operator.
  • observability — Grafana / Loki / Tempo / Mimir.
  • ingress-system — nginx ingress controller, cert-manager, external-dns.

In amira-workloads#

  • sandbox-system — agent-sandbox CRD controller, warm-pool managers.
  • sandbox-<sessionId> — short-lived sandbox-pod namespaces created per Build / Preview / Repo-import / Skill-dry-run session.
  • org-<orgId>-app-<appId>-<env> (env ∈ {dev, uat, prod}) — one namespace per app per environment for deployed apps and their companion-agent MCP servers.
  • argo-rollouts — Argo Rollouts controller.
  • image-build — Buildkit pod.
  • ingress-system — nginx ingress, cert-manager, external-dns.

11.3 Per-namespace controls (workloads cluster)#

Every sandbox-* and org-*-app-*-<env> namespace runs:

  • NetworkPolicy default-deny plus explicit egress allows for: Artifactory, ACR (image pull), Azure Key Vault (via external-secrets-operator), the Postgres + LLM-adapter endpoints (only for control-plane-marked services), and the spec-derived egress allowlist (per CROSS-4 layer 4 — for deployed apps).
  • Pod Security Standards restricted profile.
  • ResourceQuota sized per app's tier and per environment.
  • RuntimeClass = Kata-Firecracker for every pod.
  • External-secrets-operator sidecar for Key Vault-backed secret resolution.

11.4 Tenant isolation enforcement#

Tenant isolation enforces in two planes:

  • Data plane: Postgres RLS keyed by org_id + Snowflake-style immutable session attributes set on every connection (per PERSIST-5).
  • Network plane: namespace-per-org-per-app + NetworkPolicy default-deny in amira-workloads (per DEPLOY-2).

Cross-environment data leakage is therefore blocked twice (per DEPLOY-2). For BU boundaries, the same RLS engine adds a workspace_id predicate; for per-customer (when the dedicated customer-installed deployment tier ships) the boundary is the deployment itself, not a code path inside one platform.

11.5 Per-pod resource profile sketches#

(default; revisit once dogfood telemetry exists)

Pod class vCPU Memory Notes
Platform API 2 4 GB Multiple replicas behind Service
Agent runtime worker 4 8 GB Long-running; per-session memory dominated by Claude Agent SDK context cache
DBOS worker 2 4 GB Stateless poll/exec
Skill Catalog 2 4 GB Read-mostly
Audit Consumer 1 2 GB Single-writer; backpressure-tolerant
Sandbox (Next.js + FastAPI) 2 4 GB Kata microVM; tunable per pool
Deployed app 1–4 2–8 GB Per app's Helm values
Companion MCP 1 2 GB One per source app
Buildkit 4 8 GB Burst
OpenTelemetry collector 1 2 GB DaemonSet

11.6 Secrets and persistent volumes#

Secrets reach pods via external-secrets-operator pulling from Azure Key Vault. Persistent volumes are minimized: Postgres is managed (no PV); Loki / Tempo / Mimir use Azure Blob-backed object storage where supported, falling back to managed-disk PVs for Mimir's local ingester and Tempo's WAL (default; revisit). Sandbox pods are ephemeral; deployed apps are stateless except for app-owned data in their per-app database (provisioning model open per PERSIST-1 follow-up).

12. Local development#

The local stack is a docker-compose topology that mirrors production component-for-component, with the goal that a developer can clone the repo, run make dev, and have a functional Amira on localhost without Azure access.

12.1 docker-compose stack (production parity)#

Service Local impl Production equivalent
Postgres + pgvector pgvector/pgvector:pg16 container Azure Database for PostgreSQL Flexible Server
Object storage MinIO Azure Blob Storage (S3-compatible)
Secret store Local file-backed shim emulating external-secrets-operator Azure Key Vault
Container registry Local Docker registry Azure Container Registry
Dependency mirror Verdaccio (npm) + devpi (PyPI) JFrog Artifactory
Sandbox runtime Plain Docker containers (no Kata) Kata-Firecracker on AKS
Workflow engine DBOS Python (same package, against local Postgres) DBOS on managed Postgres
Argo Rollouts Skipped — helm install direct Argo Rollouts on amira-workloads
Ingress Caddy (local TLS) nginx + cert-manager + Let's Encrypt
Identity Local OIDC mock (mock-oauth2-server) Auth0 / WorkOS / customer IdP
LLM provider Anthropic API direct via ANTHROPIC_API_KEY Anthropic API (or Bedrock / Vertex / Foundry)
OpenTelemetry stack Grafana single-container dev image Grafana / Loki / Tempo / Mimir self-hosted
Skill curation scanners (Socket / Snyk / Trivy / dry-run) Skipped at install time; make scan runs the same scanners on demand Inline at every install / promotion

12.2 Mocked production features (and why)#

  • Kata-Firecracker isolation — replaced with plain Docker containers locally (developers don't run AKS Pod Sandboxing on a laptop). Trade-off: local sandboxes share the host kernel; suitable for development, never for production code execution.
  • Azure Blob Immutable Compliance Mode — replaced with MinIO (no immutability lock). Local audit chain still hash-chains rows, but the WORM property is absent. Audit-related tests pass against the chain integrity check; immutability tests run only against Azure.
  • External IdP federation — replaced by a local mock OIDC server with seeded users + orgs. Federation handshakes (SAML, customer-IdP callbacks) are exercised via integration tests in CI, not local dev.
  • Argo Rollouts BlueGreen — make dev does helm install directly; deploy gating + AC-runner runs but without the prePromotionAnalysis Service-selector flip. Local "deploy" produces a running app accessible at <app>.localtest.me (which resolves to 127.0.0.1).
  • Cross-cluster VNet peering — collapsed: both amira-platform and amira-workloads workloads run in the same compose network. The VNet boundary is exercised in CI / staging, not locally.
  • Skill curation scanners (Socket / Snyk / Trivy / Sigstore / dry-run) — disabled at the local install gate to keep make dev fast; runnable on demand via make scan.

The local stack is sufficient to build the platform itself, exercise the Spec → Build → Deploy pipeline, sign approvals, render the Compliance Matrix, and ask companion agents questions. Anything that specifically requires Azure-only behavior (immutability lock, Pod Sandboxing, Entra ID federation) is exercised in a CI staging environment that runs against actual Azure.

12.3 Seed data#

make seed loads the same FinIQ + Petcare + governance fixtures the mockup uses (/lib/mocks/*.ts as the source of truth for shape), giving every local dev environment a consistent demo state.

13. Customer-environment deployment model#

Amira's v1 architectural default is multi-tenant SaaS at amira.qdt.ai (per MTEN-1). A dedicated customer-installed deployment (e.g., Mars-Amira inside Mars's Azure subscription) is the enterprise commercial tier — same code, different deployment configuration — and is out of scope for this iteration but the platform is built so the redeploy is a configuration change, not a fork.

13.1 What gets reconfigured per deployment#

Surface Reconfigured to Default in QDT-hosted
Platform IdP Customer's IdP (Mars Entra ID / Okta / etc.) — drives users + roles directly; no federation needed Auth0 / WorkOS (federates from each customer org's IdP)
LLM provider Customer-configured via the env-var-toggle adapter — Anthropic direct, Azure OpenAI in customer subscription, AWS Bedrock, Google Vertex, Microsoft AI Foundry, or on-prem (per LLM-6) Anthropic API direct
Customer data sources Customer's data lakes (Mars QDL / QML / Q-* via Skill MCP adapters) Demo data only
Skill catalog deployment-proprietary tier Customer-admin signing key; customer-published skills (e.g., Mars's QDL/QML skills) QDT-admin key + QDT release skills
Container registry Customer's ACR or equivalent QDT's ACR
Object storage Customer's Azure Blob (or other S3-compatible) in customer subscription QDT's Azure Blob
Postgres Customer's Azure Database for PostgreSQL (or equivalent managed Postgres) QDT's instance
Secret store Customer's Key Vault (with customer's signing chains) QDT's Key Vault
DNS / hostnames Customer-chosen domain (e.g., amira.mars.com); per-app subdomain pattern preserved or replaced with per-app sub-path; cert authority configurable (Let's Encrypt or customer internal CA) amira.qdt.ai; *.apps.amira.qdt.ai
Dependency mirror Customer's curated Artifactory / Nexus QDT's Artifactory
Observability Customer-side Grafana stack (or routed via OpenTelemetry to a backend of customer choice) QDT's self-hosted Grafana

13.2 What stays the same#

  • Two-cluster split (platform + workloads).
  • Postgres + pgvector schema, RLS rules, immutable session attribute pattern.
  • Hash-chained audit ledger + WORM Merkle anchor pattern (Azure Blob Immutable Compliance Mode is the reference, but any WORM-compliant object store satisfies the contract).
  • DBOS workflow engine, Claude Agent SDK runtime, MCP skill format with Amira manifest overlay.
  • agent-sandbox CRD with Kata-Firecracker, warm pools.
  • Helm + Argo Rollouts BlueGreen deploy with AC-runner + prePromotionAnalysis.
  • OBO via RFC 8693 Token Exchange; three-field actor + causedBy audit attribution.
  • Spec capability graph + Compliance Matrix re-evaluation.
  • Per-tenant config record (per MTEN-2) loaded at session start — in a single-tenant deployment the config simply has one tenant.

13.3 What isn't supported#

  • License enforcement, feature-gating, tier-based entitlement — the platform has no runtime license-key check, no feature flag tied to a license tier, no expiration-triggered read-only mode, no phone-home enforcement (per 00-context.md). Entitlement is governed contractually. If AMS lapses the customer keeps a working perpetual build but stops receiving updates.
  • Per-user BYOK — v1 only supports per-org BYOK (per LLM-6).
  • Subscription-OAuth proxy for LLMs — permanently rejected (per LLM-6, Anthropic Feb 2026 ToS).
  • Cloud lock-in to Azure — the platform runs on AKS today and should remain portable to other Kubernetes flavors with a configuration change. Avoiding Azure-Monitor / Application Insights / Log Analytics is the structural reason the observability stack is Grafana-based (per OBS-3).
  • Local-agent topology (user runs the agent on their own machine) — out of scope (per 00-context.md / LLM-6 option 4).

13.4 Deployment-time configuration registry#

A per-deployment + per-org config record (per MTEN-2) is loaded at session start and supplies: skills allowlist, governance roles, vocabulary, compliance standards, prompt fragments, audit kinds. Tenant-specific tools install through the skill catalog's deployment-proprietary tier (per SKILL-3). Fork-driven customization is rejected.

14. Open architectural risks#

Risks the platform is choosing not to solve in v1, why that's safe for now, and what would force a revisit.

14.1 Single-Postgres concentration#

One Postgres family carries application state, DBOS workflow state, audit outboxes, and the audit ledger. A Postgres outage is a platform-wide outage.

Why safe — Azure Database for PostgreSQL Flexible Server with geo-redundant backup + point-in-time restore is a managed substrate operated by Microsoft. v1 expected concurrency (Mars-rollout scale, ~200–500 events/sec peak per ORCH-1) is an order of magnitude under the chain-write ceiling. RUNTIME-1 picked DBOS-on-shared-Postgres specifically to keep operational surface low.

Trigger to revisit — Sustained chain-write throughput >1k events/sec for a rolling 24h window (WAL-tail migration), or approach to ~5k events/sec (per-project chain sharding). For workflow workload: separate the DBOS Postgres from the audit Postgres if the triple-workload contention surfaces.

14.2 Single audit consumer#

One global Audit Consumer in v1 (per ORCH-1). Consumer outage delays audit visibility for every project.

Why safe — The hash chain is intrinsically serial (one writer to the chain). Consumer outage doesn't block business writes; only audit visibility lags. SKIP LOCKED degrades gracefully.

Trigger to revisit — Sustained backpressure or consumer operational fragility. Migration is partition-key-per-consumer, not architectural redesign.

14.3 Single-agent ReAct loop without verifier#

Day-one Build Agent runs single-agent without a verifier sub-agent (per AGENT-TOPO-1). Compliance re-eval shares context budget with the main loop.

Why safe — Cheaper, fewer moving parts. Compliance Matrix re-eval is bounded; published research shows verifier sub-agents help mostly when error rates are unacceptable.

Trigger to revisit — Compliance re-eval starves the main loop's context budget (measured), or single-agent error rate is unacceptable on dogfood metrics.

14.4 Forward-only rollback in v1.0#

v1.0 ships forward-only rollback (helm rollback <release> <revision>). v1.5 adds Argo Rollouts BlueGreen + paired companion-agent version-pin flip atomicity (per DEPLOY-5).

Why safe — Helm release history is preserved per app. Forward-only is acceptable when ACs gate every promotion.

Trigger to revisit — Customer requirement for atomic rollback, or operational pain from manual companion-agent re-pin.

14.5 Public anchor publication not implemented#

Audit anchor is sealed in Azure Blob Immutable Compliance Mode in QDT's subscription, but not published to a public transparency log.

Why safe — Cohasset-assessed Azure Blob Compliance Mode meets SEC 17a-4(f) / FINRA 4511(c) / CFTC 1.31(c) without public publication.

Trigger to revisit — A regulator or customer specifically asks for public verifiability.

14.6 Single greenfield stack (Next.js + FastAPI)#

v1 commits to one stack for full Build Agent capability (per BUILD-1). Imported repos in non-Next/FastAPI stacks are host-only (degraded experience).

Why safe — Lovable-style narrow lock-in is the deliberate quality trade. The cost to add a stack is bounded (~1 dev-month).

Trigger to revisit — A paying customer requires a different greenfield stack.

14.7 Per-user BYOK deferred#

v1 supports per-org BYOK only (per LLM-6). Per-user BYOK is a future feature.

Why safe — Org-level BYOK matches the org-as-tenant model (MTEN-1) and covers the volume-economics use case.

Trigger to revisit — Power-user demand for per-user keys, or org-level BYOK proves operationally awkward.

14.8 No multi-LLM-provider in v1#

The LLM adapter exposes Anthropic-family models only in v1; OpenAI / Gemini / others are Phase 2 (per LLM-6).

Why safe — Anthropic models cover Build Agent quality. The adapter shape (env-var-toggle) preserves the option without code change.

Trigger to revisit — A customer specifically requires another provider, or model-quality gap on a target task.

14.9 Dedicated customer-installed deployment is parallel offering#

The dedicated customer-installed enterprise tier (Mars-Amira inside Mars's Azure subscription) remains available but is out of scope for this iteration (per MTEN-1). Multi-tenant SaaS is the v1 default.

Why safe — Same code, different deployment configuration. The platform is built so the redeploy is a configuration change, not a fork (§13).

Trigger to revisit — Commercial demand validates the dedicated tier; until then, the SaaS shape is the priority.

14.10 Companion-agent prompt customization not user-editable in v1#

v1 ships pure-auto companion-agent synthesis (per AGENT-1 follow-ups). Explicit prompt customization is Phase 2.

Why safe — Synthesis from spec FRs + ACs covers the demo and early production cases. Hand-edit creates an ownership question about the SKILL.md across deploys.

Trigger to revisit — Customer demand for branded / customized companion-agent voice.

14.11 Time-travel UI in Canvas deferred#

Per-build snapshots / checkpoints surface in Canvas as a time-travel UI is Phase 2 (per BUILD-4 follow-ups). The CAS layer + Git tagging already store the necessary data.

Why safe — Build-session checkpoints (feature 14.5) preserve work; Git tags + repo browsing cover the recovery use case.

Trigger to revisit — User research surfaces strong demand.
